articles.title: The German Local Manifesto Project (GLMP): A new data source for studying local party politics
articles.abstract: Local politics remains comparatively understudied in political science, partly due to limited data on party competition at the municipal level. This research note introduces the German Local Manifesto Project (GLMP), a new dataset of German local election manifestos that expands the empirical infrastructure for studying programmatic competition in municipalities. The dataset contains 2307 manifestos from 306 political actors across 248 municipalities between 1989 and 2024, covering both national party branches and Independent Local Lists (ILL). Compared with existing collections of local manifestos, GLMP provides broader coverage of political actors and municipal contexts. The data allow scholars to analyze ideological positioning and policy priorities in local elections. An illustrative analysis demonstrates how the dataset can be used to compare ideological dispersion between ILL and national party branches. By providing large-scale manifesto data for German municipalities, GLMP opens new opportunities for research on local party competition and political representation.

articles.title: The personal efficacy of party youth wing members
articles.authors: Henrik Bech Seeberg, Duncan McDonnell, Sofia Ammassari, Niklas Bolin, Reinhard Heinisch, Ann-Cathrine Jungar, Marco Valbruzzi, Carsten Wegscheider, Annika Werner
articles.abstract: Although young people are said to be increasingly withdrawing from participation in political parties, some still join because they believe they can influence them to achieve change. We examine this sense of personal efficacy among contemporary youth wing members and ask: how is youth wing members’ personal efficacy associated with their activity levels and membership length, and with intra-party democracy and youth wing integration into the party? To do so, we combine the Political Party Database with data from the YOUMEM project, the largest cross-national survey of youth wing members conducted to date, covering ∼3600 members of 12 party youth wings in six democracies. We find that higher levels of personal efficacy are associated in particular with individuals being more active; being in a youth wing which is well integrated into the party; and in a context of strong intra-party democracy. Our results thus suggest how parties can foster young members’ personal efficacy and nurture democratically engaged citizens.

articles.title: Contesting reputational advantages: Issue ownership and negative campaigning
articles.abstract: Research on issue-based negative campaigning typically emphasizes issue salience and parties’ own issue strengths. This paper shifts the focus to the targets of attacks. We argue that negative campaigning on policy issues is systematically structured by the competence of the opponent, as parties seek to challenge rivals’ reputational advantages within specific issue domains. Using a dyadic dataset of party press releases from five Austrian national election campaigns (2006–2019), combined with survey-based measures of perceived issue competence, we show that parties are significantly more likely to direct negative messages at highly competent opponents. In contrast, sender-party competence and voter issue salience do not consistently shape targeting patterns. These findings suggest that issue-based negative campaigning is driven less by parties’ own issue strengths than by their opponents’ relative standing, highlighting how attacks serve as a strategy of reputational contestation in issue competition.

What Do We Get from Two-Way Fixed Effects Regressions? Implications from Numerical Equivalence
articles.abstract: This paper develops numerical and causal interpretations of two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regressions in settings with nonbinary, nonstaggered treatments and time-varying covariates. Using the equivalence between TWFE and pooled first-difference (FD) regressions, I express the TWFE coefficient as a weighted average of FD coefficients across all horizons, clarifying how short- and long-run changes contribute to the estimate. Causal interpretation of the TWFE coefficient relies on common trends assumptions at all horizons simultaneously, whereas each FD coefficient relies on the assumption only at its own horizon. This structure opens the identifying assumptions to empirical scrutiny: I propose diagnostic procedures that assess common trends horizon by horizon, and illustrate them by reexamining TWFE estimates of minimum-wage effects on employment.

articles.title: Quantile Treatment Effects in Difference-in-Discontinuities Designs
articles.abstract: This paper studies identification and doubly robust (DR) estimation of quantile treatment effects (QTEs) in difference-in-discontinuities (diff-in-disc) designs when a new treatment is introduced in the post period and a confounding discontinuous policy is present in both periods. We show that QTEs are point identified under a conditional stable-distributional-effect assumption for the confounding treatment, a restriction that is analogous to the distributional parallel trends assumption in the recent difference-in-differences literature. We then propose a DR estimator and inference procedure that remain valid when either the outcome regression or the propensity score model is correctly specified, while avoiding high-dimensional nonparametric adjustment for covariates in the local estimation setting. We establish asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator, and Monte Carlo simulations illustrate its double-robustness and good finite-sample performance. In an application to Italian municipal fiscal data (Grembi et al. 2016),, the estimates suggest that relaxing fiscal constraints increases deficits primarily over the lower and central portions of the distribution, shifting municipalities from surplus or near balance into moderate deficits—a distributional pattern not captured by mean effects.

articles.title: Global factors for local shocks in a data-scarce environment: with an application to regional fiscal multipliers in Italy
articles.authors: Giuseppe Cavaliere, Luca Fanelli, Marco Mazzali
articles.abstract: We propose a novel econometric methodology for Structural Vector Autoregressions with external instruments (‘proxy-SVARs’ or ‘SVAR-IVs’) in panel data characterized by strong cross-sectional dependence, dynamic heterogeneity, and limited availability of direct external instruments for the shocks of interest. For each unit, we specify a Factor-Augmented proxy-SVAR (‘proxy-FA-SVAR’) that incorporates factors summarizing cross-sectional information from the non-policy variables of the system. The effects of the policy shocks are then recovered indirectly by estimating unit-specific policy reaction functions through a Minimum Distance approach. Identification relies on global instruments for the non-policy shocks; that is, proxies common to all units in the panel, internally constructed from a separate SVAR estimated on factors for the policy and non-policy variables. These global instruments can be complemented with local (idiosyncratic) instruments constructed from auxiliary unit-level SVARs. Their joint use renders the proxy-FA-SVARs overidentified and therefore statistically testable. We illustrate the methodology by estimating government spending multipliers for Italian NUTS-2 regions using annual data. The global and local instruments for the regional output shocks are obtained from Blanchard-Perotti-type SVARs.

articles.title: Bootstrapping likelihood-ratio-type tests based on convex M-estimation
articles.abstract: We consider likelihood-ratio-type statistics for testing restrictions on parameters built from a convex M-estimation criterion. In general, these statistics are not asymptotically pivotal. We propose a general simple nonparametric bootstrap procedure that yields asymptotically valid critical and p-values. The method modifies the bootstrap objective function to mimic what happens under the null hypothesis. A Monte-Carlo study illustrates that our method controls level well and is powerful.

articles.title: Do electoral polls explain the winner–loser gap in political trust? A panel study on polls, election results, and political trust in Belgium
articles.abstract: There is an ongoing debate on whether elections boost levels of political trust across the board or exclusively among the “winners” of the elections. The subsequent question is who exactly can be defined as the “winner” of a specific election. In the current study, we report on a panel survey that was conducted both before and after the 2024 general elections in Belgium. Results show that the experience of elections tends to boost levels of political trust, but this effect is stronger among the perceived winners of the elections. Most importantly, we find that this effect depends more strongly on a comparison with published public opinion poll results than on a comparison to the result of previous elections. We argue, therefore, that the winner–loser debate should take into account the effects of polls and mass media communication in shaping voters’ expectations when operationalising winning and losing.

articles.authors: Josephine Lukito, Yini Zhang, Bin Chen, Stephen Prochaska, Meredith L. Pruden, Yunkang Yang, Wei Zhong, Megan A. Brown, Ross Dahlke, Jason Greenfield, Jiyoun Suk, Porismita Borah
articles.abstract: This study examines how seven right-leaning media organizations utilize cross-platformization strategies to reach audiences across multiple platforms; in this case, Twitter and Truth Social. Focusing on both content volume and story packaging, we collect right-leaning media organizations’ social media posts and content from the 2022 U.S. midterm election. Combining computational and qualitative methods, we find that outlets posted only a small share of total stories across the two platforms and were selective in their content, often posting only on Twitter or Truth Social. For content posted on both platforms, the outlets posted content that ideologically aligned with the users of that platform. More specifically, right-leaning outlets on Truth Social tailored their posts to ideologically aligned users.

articles.title: Are they virtue-signalling or sincere? The impact of perceived motives on the effectiveness of online collective action
articles.authors: Lisette Yip, Emma F. Thomas, Hawa Muhammad Farid, M. Noor Tahir
articles.abstract: Social media is an important tool used by supporters of modern social movements to persuade others to participate. However, people who engage in online collective action often face speculation about their motives and may be perceived as acting for self-serving reasons. How do these perceptions impact the effectiveness of collective action? In three experiments ( N = 916), participants viewed posts (Study 1) or an immersive social media feed (Studies 2–3) where a user encouraged them to take action for a political cause. They stated that they acted out of genuine concern (autonomous motivation), to avoid guilt and social disapproval (controlled motivation), or did not specify (baseline). Participants who viewed controlled-motivated posts perceived the user as less autonomously motivated and were therefore less likely to socially identify as supporters or take collective action. Thus, movements will be more effective at mobilising (online) support when they are seen to arise from autonomous motives.

articles.abstract: This editorial article traces the shift in the political economy of climate policy from a paradigm centered on carbon pricing to one increasingly defined by industrial policy. It maps the distinct models of green industrial policy emerging across jurisdictions, examines the implications of this industrial turn for low- and middle-income countries—particularly in relation to structural dependency and extraction—and sets out a research agenda for understanding the questions raised by this shift.

articles.title: A Few Good Women? Gendered Socialization and Norms of Civilian Protection in United States Military Training
articles.authors: Andrew Bell, Thomas Gift, Jonathan Monten, Chiara Ruffa
articles.abstract: Many professionalized militaries seek to train combatants in “norms of restraint” (NoR) based on international legal principles of noncombatant immunity. Does training in NoR affect the attitudes of women and men toward the protection of civilians differently? Drawing on unique surveys of United States Army officer cadets at the US Military Academy (USMA), we find that while women and men held similar attitudes at the start of their academy training, women’s attitudes shifted more toward civilian restraint, despite receiving identical formal training in international humanitarian law (IHL), combat ethics, and officership. To explore the causes of this gender divergence, we conduct open-ended, in-depth interviews with former USMA cadets. We find that socialization at USMA is deeply gendered, and that differences in norm socialization are linked to a prevailing “gender order” constructed by formal and informal rules, practices, and norms that attribute distinct roles to women and men in military settings. Despite the seemingly “ungendered” nature of USMA’s intensive training in IHL and combat ethics, this gender order creates different socialization experiences for women and men, resulting in divergent attitudes toward civilian restraint. These findings shed light on how socialization and gender interact to shape combatant attitudes toward NoR, and are especially notable given the USMA’s status as the US Army’s “flagship of ethics education.”

articles.title: Elections, Government Turnover, and Citizen Acceptance of Political Violence: Evidence from Election Panel Surveys in Zambia and Kenya
articles.abstract: Elections in unconsolidated democracies are contentious moments with heightened risks of violence. Although elections offer hope to the politically marginalized, ruling parties often enjoy insurmountable advantages, sometimes leading to frustration and concerns for groups and citizens’ exclusion from power. How do elections shape citizens’ acceptance of political violence in unconsolidated democracies? Furthermore, can government turnovers reduce the support for political violence among citizens previously excluded from political power? We argue that citizens respond both to electoral outcomes and their perception of the electoral process when updating their attitudes on political violence. We leverage an original panel survey of the Zambia 2021 election to measure changes in attitudes to political violence before and after an election. Because the 2021 election resulted in a turnover of power, it provides a critical test to evaluate updated perceptions amid political change. We show that election winners reduce their support for political violence and election losers increase their acceptance of violence, even in the case of a turnover. We also show that increased perceptions of election quality reduce the acceptance of violence. Extending our study to an analysis of original panel data from the Kenyan 2017 election (a case without a turnover and low election quality), we find similar patterns.

articles.title: Colonial Legacies and the Dynamics of Opposition: How Factional Power Shapes Cycles of Moderation and Radicalization
articles.abstract: This article explains why opposition movements in the Middle East cycle between radicalization and moderation over long periods. I argue that twentieth-century colonization shaped both exclusionary state institutions and radical opposition groups, structuring how later episodes of inclusion and exclusion influenced movement strategies. The paper explains subsequent oscillations through a single core mechanism: shifting factional balances of power. State inclusion and exclusion redistribute influence between moderates and radicals, generating shifts between confrontation and accommodation. I develop and evaluate the theory through longitudinal process tracing of the Muslim Brothers in Egypt and the Iraqi Communist Party, supplemented by shadow cases illustrating colonial presence (Palestine) and absence (Turkey), using evidence from 96 semistructured interviews, archival materials, and participant observation conducted between 2021 and 2024 in Palestine, Iraq, and Turkey. By foregrounding temporality and factional dynamics, the article reframes debates on Islamist moderation and authoritarian durability as path-dependent and iterative processes rather than linear transformations.

articles.title: Exercise or Extra Fries? Behavioral Drivers of Obesity Over the Life Cycle,
articles.authors: Neha Bairoliya, Ray Miller, Vegard M Nygaard
articles.abstract: As America faces an obesity epidemic and its economic consequences, the factors driving weight variation across the U.S. population remain unclear, especially since these differences extend well beyond commonly studied channels like income or education. We leverage a unique thirty-year panel of U.S. registered nurses to examine the changes in body mass index (BMI) with age, the impact of lifestyle choices on body weight in adulthood, and the role of inherited metabolic traits and childhood preference formation. Our empirical findings reveal that among individuals who enter adulthood with a healthy body mass, those in the top diet quality or exercise deciles at age thirty are roughly 50% more likely to maintain a healthy BMI and avoid morbidities three decades later, compared to those in the bottom deciles. To better understand the drivers of weight gain, we propose a novel structural framework of endogenous BMI evolution where initial heterogeneity is amplified by behaviors to explain much of the observed divergence in weight. Counterfactual experiments using the model indicate that initial conditions, such as fixed metabolic types, account for at least one-third of the variance in weight at older ages. While course correction through behaviors can only partially compensate for poor initial conditions at the onset of adulthood, we find that promoting healthy behaviors in adults can reduce total health care expenses by at least 8% annually.

articles.title: The Fall of Constantinople and the Rise of the West,
articles.abstract: The Renaissance era in Western Europe was marked by a flourishing of economic and cultural life that gave rise to numerous discoveries and inventions. This paper studies the role played by Greek knowledge in this process. Using a newly constructed dataset on Greek migrants in Europe after the fall of Constantinople in 1453, I show that a Greek presence in the second half of the fifteenth century increased city growth in the sixteenth century. In terms of mechanisms, I find that a Greek presence increased the available knowledge stock in astronomy, mathematics, medicine, and humanistic subjects – fields in which ancient Greek and Byzantine knowledge was especially advanced. Finally, I document an increase in upper-tail human capital and inventions in these cities. My findings thus show the important role played by Greek migrants in disseminating knowledge and the positive impact that Greek knowledge exerted on city growth in the early modern period.

articles.title: Employment and Community: Socioeconomic Cooperation and Its Breakdown
articles.abstract: We model the interplay of employment relations and community-based interactions among workers and managers. Employment relations can be either tough (where workers are monitored intensively and obtain few rents, and managers do not provide informal favors for workers) or soft (where there is less monitoring, more worker rents, and more workplace favor exchange). Both workers and managers also exert effort in providing community public goods. The threat of losing access to public goods can motivate managers to keep employment soft; conversely, the threat of losing future employment or future workers’ trust can motivate workers and managers to provide effort in the community. Corporate tax cuts; improved worker monitoring; automation, outsourcing, and offshoring; declines in the minimum wage; and opportunities for residential segregation or for privatizing community-provided services can make both workers and managers worse-off by undermining soft employment relations and community cooperation.

articles.title: The Game of Making Money: How Rural Migrant Delivery Riders Are Motivated to Work Very Long Hours in China
articles.authors: Yu Feng, Paul Waley, Jie Shen
articles.abstract: What motivates rural migrant delivery riders in China to work very long hours, and how are they managed by their working platforms? This paper investigates the motivations of rural migrant riders in Shanghai to engage in continuous work and examines the management strategies employed by their platforms. Drawing on participant observation and interviews with rural migrant riders working for the two largest on‐demand food delivery platforms in China, this paper finds that gamified algorithmic controls incentivize riders' labour. Driven by strict working performance assessment, Shanghai riders are attracted by three types of games: the everyday game of assessing work performance, the game played with their working platforms and the game played among riders. Building on these findings, this article identifies three defining features that condition consent from workers within the platform labour regime: its temporal fragmentation, informational asymmetry and hyper‐individualization. The gamification process ultimately aligns with broader trends of datafication within the online food delivery sector. These findings contribute to understandings of labour games in platform economies and offer insights into the emergence of ‘sticky labour’ in exploitative working environments. In doing so, it underscores the contingent, situated nature of labour motivation in the platform economy and extends Burawoy's analysis to digital labour regimes.

articles.title: Why Stay? Local Opportunity Anchoring and Gendered Immobility in Peri‐Urban China
articles.abstract: Why women remain in split households cannot be inferred from residence alone: staying may be desired, accepted, or constrained. Drawing on two interview rounds a year apart and later online follow‐up with 10 women in a peri‐urban Yunnan village whose partners worked elsewhere, this article examines how staying was sustained as local tourism contracted. Six sustained employment‐based staying through other local jobs; three remained through care, schooling, and remittances; one migrated as high household expenses coincided with reduced childcare demands. We define local opportunity anchoring as the employment‐based pathway through which work within commuting range sustains the feasibility of residence already organised around care, schooling, and hukou: nearby jobs become usable when social networks convey job information, care arrangements make employment feasible, and earnings meet household‐specific needs. The findings separate the feasibility of staying from women's orientations and show how life‐course positions, linked lives, and peri‐urban accessibility shape divergent trajectories.

articles.title: Career Pathways in the Global Labour Market: Non‐European Master's Graduates in Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom
articles.abstract: This paper examines the career pathways of international STEM and business master's alumni who graduated in Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom, based on 28 in‐depth interviews with international master's graduates from India, China, and Iran. The findings indicate that the career pathways and labour market destinations of non‐European master's graduates are significantly influenced by the contextual conditions present in both home and host countries. In contrast to the clear trend in Germany and Italy towards the host labour market or other Western‐oriented markets, the data from the United Kingdom indicates that contextual conditions resulted in either a successful transition to the host labour market or a return to the home country. The pursuit of career pathways is also significantly influenced by conditions prevailing in the home country. However, the findings of this study further indicate that these effects are subject to variation depending on the contextual conditions of the respective host country.

articles.title: Local Enrollment or Cross‐Regional Portability? Public Healthcare Service Utilization and Older Migrants' Settlement Intentions in China
articles.authors: Cuiying Huang, Zheng Luo, Ye Liu, Zhixin Feng
articles.abstract: China has substantially reformed its medical insurance system to enable direct cross‐regional settlement of medical expenses since the late 2000s, yet little is known about how different forms of medical insurance participation—local enrollment vs. cross‐regional portability—differentially shape older migrants' settlement intentions. To address this gap, using nationally representative survey data on 5002 older migrants who have reached the statutory retirement age, this study examines how public healthcare service utilization influences older migrants' settlement intentions in China. Public healthcare service utilization is measured using four indicators: participation in destination‐based medical insurance, participation in origin‐based medical insurance with direct settlement at the destination, establishment of a local resident health record, and participation in health education activities. Multinomial probit models are used to account for the categorical nature of settlement intentions: no intention, short‐term intentions, and long‐term intentions. Model results show that older migrants enrolled in destination‐based medical insurance are more likely to express long‐term settlement intentions, whereas those relying on origin‐based insurance with cross‐regional settlement tend to exhibit short‐term intentions. In addition, older migrants who have established a local resident health record are more likely to express long‐term settlement intentions. Furthermore, origin–destination disparities in the quantity and quality of medical service provision significantly moderate the association between medical insurance participation and older migrants' settlement intentions. Our findings advance understanding of older migrants' settlement intentions by revealing the divergent effects of local enrollment and cross‐regional portability on long‐term vs. short‐term settlement, and by highlighting the moderating role of origin–destination disparities in medical service provision, with implications for deepening cross‐regional settlement reforms to better facilitate the long‐term urban integration of older migrants.

articles.title: The Residential Mobility of Mid‐Term Temporary Populations: Personal Trajectories and Sociospatial Patterns in Rome
articles.abstract: This article examines how medium‐term temporary dwellers—who have been living in a city for months or a few years without planning to settle in the long term—impact upon intra‐urban residential mobility and sociospatial inequalities in Southern European contexts. Building on debates on residential mobility, (im)mobilities and temporary urban populations, the paper argues that these groups should be treated as a distinct and influential mobility actor. Empirically, the study draws on original mixed‐methods evidence from Rome, combining a survey and follow‐up interviews to link motivations for arrival, housing practices, and intra‐urban relocations. Rome is discussed as a relevant Southern European case where post‐crisis housing‐market restructuring, uneven accessibility and the expansion of platform‐mediated rental circuits intensify competition for centrally located housing. The findings show that temporary dwellers' residential movements and strategies contribute to neighbourhood change and can reinforce displacement pressures and unequal access to central and semi‐central areas, thereby shaping broader patterns of residential mobility for the overall resident population.

articles.title: Discretionary disclosure and electoral accountability
articles.abstract: Politicians often have discretion over what policy information to reveal to the public. This paper develops a formal model comparing electoral accountability under mandatory and discretionary disclosure. I identify a fundamental trade-off between detection − where voters directly observe wrongdoing − and inference − where voters penalize the suspicious absence of information. Mandates facilitate detection but eliminate the strategic signal embedded in discretionary disclosure. Mandates weaken the connection between silence and possible wrongdoing, effectively exonerating the incumbent in voters’ inferences. The model demonstrates that when the baseline probability of information transmission is high, the inference-based mechanism constrains rent-seeking more effectively than the detection-based mechanism. Consequently, disclosure mandates can paradoxically weaken electoral discipline: by making silence less informative, they undermine voters’ ability to draw inferences from silence, even while increasing the overall probability that voters observe policy outcomes.

articles.title: Sarah Sunn Bush and Jennifer Hadden. 2025. Crowded Out: The Competitive Landscape of Contemporary International NGOs. (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
Signaling for aid? Effects of signing democracy-related provisions in preferential trade agreements
articles.abstract: Aid for Trade has been a key instrument established by donor agencies to support the implementation of trade-related commitments to the World Trade Organization and preferential trade agreements (PTAs). Yet relatively little is known about the links between the signature of non-trade provisions in PTAs and foreign aid. Democracy-related provisions are of particular relevance, as they potentially offer a unique mechanism for democratic donors to link good governance criteria to economic interests. I theorize that democracy-related provisions can lead to increases in aid through establishing institutional frameworks that enhance long-term cooperation and monitoring. By contrast, I do not expect recipients to receive additional foreign aid support to reward credible commitments to democratization, to implement such provisions, nor as a by-product of deep trade commitments. Overall, I find support for these hypotheses, estimating a staggered difference-in-differences model over 100 mixed-regime country pairs from 1966 to 2019. This paper demonstrates that signing democracy-related provisions can enable signatories to secure aid deals, although not aimed at democratization or the implementation of such provisions.

articles.title: Gendered Political Violence in Transitional Moments: The Cases of Bangladesh and Iran
articles.abstract: Women’s rights advocates and movements play an important role during political transitions, shaping feminist outcomes following these transitions. Women are also often at the forefront of many pro-democratic mobilizations and struggles for political change (Baldez 2002; Goetz 2009; Viterna and Fallon 2008; Waylen 2007; 2011). Yet this participation is not without costs, and one core cost remains undertheorized in the literature: targeted violence against women precisely because of their gender and political engagement.

articles.title: Violence Against Women Political Activists
articles.abstract: In the last decade, research on violence against women in politics (VAWIP) has increased significantly. First identified by women activists in the Global South, VAWIP refers to behaviors that specifically target women as women by pressuring them to leave politics (Krook and Sanín 2016). Activists in Bolivia and later in other regions of the Global South first called attention to VAWIP in the late 1990s and early 2000s, when countries around the world began adopting gender quotas to increase the presence of women in government (Krook 2019). Most scholarship in this area has focused on violence targeting women candidates and elected officials (Collignon and Rüdig 2020; Dalton 2021; Håkansson 2021; Herrick et al. 2021; Raney and Collier 2024; Schneider and Carroll 2020). Attention to women in formal politics is warranted given their important representational role. Women’s presence in politics is a necessary first step to achieve political change and advance women’s interests (Beckwith 2011).

articles.title: Systemic Imbalances in Integrity Management Systems: A Meso‐Level Framework From Four Corruption Scandals
articles.authors: Georgios Kominis, Adina Dudau, Alvise Favotto, Denisse Rodriguez‐Olivari
articles.abstract: Integrity management systems (IMSs) are increasingly promoted to embed ethical conduct, mitigate corruption risks, and strengthen organizational accountability. Yet empirical evidence on their effectiveness remains sparse and contradictory, offering little insight into how these systems operate in practice and why they often fail in heavily formalized organizational settings. This paper addresses that gap by developing a meso‐level framework for diagnosing systemic imbalances in IMSs. Drawing on systems theory and management control literature, we conceptualize IMSs as an integrity management package structured through four levers: belief, boundary, diagnostic, and interactive systems of control. We deploy this framework through an explanatory, multi‐case design spanning four major corruption scandals in infrastructure, defense, healthcare, and banking in the UK, Italy, Greece, and the Nordic–Baltic region, drawing on a triangulated dataset built through systematic web scraping. The cross‐case analysis shows that integrity failures are not explained simply by the absence of formal controls, but by recurring imbalances among control levers. Organizations tend to privilege boundary and diagnostic systems, such as rules, procedures, monitoring, and performance metrics, while under‐investing in belief and interactive systems that should enable ethical culture, dialogue, challenge, and learning. We theorize this imbalance as a compliance façade: formally robust but weakly embedded in organizational practice. The paper thereby reframes the compliance versus values debate in ethics scholarship, offering the first empirically grounded, cross‐sectoral model of how integrity is embedded, sustained, and undermined in organizations, with implications for redesigning IMSs across public, private, and hybrid settings.

articles.title: The problem of intelligence in International Relations theory
articles.abstract: States spy. Yet International Relations (IR) theory has no systematic account of intelligence. I make three arguments. First, realist IR theories are too narrow to theorize intelligence as the complex social practice it is. Realism renders intelligence invisible or reduces it to a single instrumental raison d’état logic. Second, the English School’s societal approach opens the way for theorizing intelligence as instrument of normative practice. Extending Adam Watson’s raison de système to intelligence, grounded in the intelligence–diplomacy relationship and corroborated by an emerging lex specialis , establishes that intelligence helps constitute international society rather than merely operating within it. Third, the societal approach does not exhaust the subject. Raison d’humanité names a third logic – intelligence in the service of justice – and critical approaches deepen the account by asking whose survival, whose order, and whose humanity the framework serves. The three logics are in permanent tension and tend toward a rough hierarchy, reflecting political choice rather than structural necessity. This analysis raises a question for future research: whether intelligence qualifies as a primary institution of international society – a practice whose place is not at the margins of world politics but at its center. Where there are spies, there is society.

articles.title: Accidental architects: self-effacing objectives in international relations
articles.abstract: International relations scholarship typically assumes that states achieve their objectives through deliberate, strategic action. This article develops an alternative account: many state objectives are self-effacing – they cannot be attained directly, but only as byproducts of other pursuits. I argue that this dynamic is especially likely under interdependence, where networks emerge through the voluntary participation of new entrants. Under such conditions, overt bids for future leverage provoke resistance, hedging, and duplication. Where durable structural advantage does materialize, it tends to arise indirectly, as the unintended result of principled state commitments, or of nonstate actors pursuing goals unrelated to geopolitics. I illustrate the argument through cases in global finance and global supply chains, showing how leverage repeatedly emerges from processes no state intended. Finally, I turn to foreign influence campaigns to demonstrate how states can nonetheless design conditions conducive to ‘welcome byproducts.’ Yet doing so requires relinquishing some control. The result is a reframing of strategy in international relations: dominance proves most likely when it is not openly pursued.

articles.title: Anarchy versus organization: how the social science of International Relations emerged from controversies over war, evolution, and Darwinism
articles.abstract: In this article, we show how IR’s central debate about international anarchy emerged from controversies over war, evolution and Darwinism that took place around 1900. It was a chiefly European debate between apologists of war – polemically called ‘Social Darwinists’ – and proponents of a ‘scientific pacifism,’ in particular the sociologist Jacques Novicow and the peace activist Alfred H. Fried. Apologists of war cited theories of evolution to portray international politics as an agonistic struggle among states, civilizations or races. Arguing from that premise, they naturalized political violence and imperialism. Scientific pacifists cited theories of evolution to show that anarchy was malleable and could be overcome through international organization. In their view, evolution rewarded cooperation of humankind in its struggle against the forces of nature. Ever since, evolutionary theorizing has returned to IR debates. Most defining, as we argue, has been the controversy between Kenneth N. Waltz and Alexander Wendt over the consequences of international anarchy. It was equally a debate about the right interpretation of what evolution implies for international politics. We conclude that evolutionary theory has been a lifetime companion of disciplinary IR, intimately related to the anarchy theme.

articles.title: The international and transnational politics of the far right: an emergent research program
articles.abstract: This article offers a state-of-the-art review of a new and growing research program in International Relations (IR) that analyzes the far right’s inter- and transnational politics. Responding to the rise of far-right leaders, parties, and movements worldwide, this nascent literature sheds light on the inter- and transnational drivers, patterns, connections, and effects of far-right politics. To further consolidate and develop this emerging research program, as this article argues, it is imperative to integrate this literature into a wider framework that delineates different analytical approaches and research agendas. For this purpose, the article identifies and examines five research strands: (1) foreign and security policy, (2) international thought, (3) the global causes of the rise of the far right, (4) trans- and international collaboration, and (5) international norms, institutions, and orders. It appraises their different analytical perspectives and insights, connects each research strand with various IR paradigms, subdisciplines, and literatures, and identifies unexplored lines of inquiry. Thereby, the article aims to broaden and diversify the theoretical, empirical, and methodological scope of this research program and to further facilitate synergies between IR and far-right studies. It then discusses a series of limitations and challenges facing this research program and proposes a level-of-analysis approach to advance it.

Privacy Asymmetries in Digital Public Mobility: Trust and the Perceived Value of Personal Data
articles.authors: Mónica Humeres, Alexandra Davidoff, Teresa Correa, Claudia López
articles.abstract: As algorithmic platforms increasingly mediate public service delivery, data‐driven systems shape how citizens experience trust and privacy while generating digital traces that inform policy decisions. In the context of public mobility, these dynamics manifest through routine interactions with systems that track movement, log behavior, and process personal information, transforming everyday travel into a site of data extraction with policy implications. This study investigates how individuals in Chile interpret and respond to digital transport systems, focusing on their concerns about data privacy, institutional trust, and the value of the data they generate. Drawing on interviews ( N = 27) and six focus groups ( N = 48), the paper uses the notion of privacy asymmetries to characterize the uneven dispositions users hold across three dimensions: (1) between functionality trust in digital platforms and data privacy concerns; (2) between acceptance of data collection practices by private companies and by the state, and (3) across demographic lines, particularly gender. These asymmetries reflect how historical legacies, political context, and sociodemographic categories shape trust and skepticism toward data use in public systems.

articles.title: Trust in the Machine? Practitioner Perspectives on the Role of AI in Online Content Moderation
articles.authors: Elena Martellozzo, Kylie McCarthy, Megan Trafford, Emmanuel Adinkrah, Paul Bleakley
articles.abstract: The scale and volume of user‐generated content produced in the Web 2.0 era have led to content moderation becoming an essential aspect of most online platforms' business models. This form of digital labour is often performed by human content moderators (CMs) in the Global South, however, artificial intelligence (AI) technology has increasingly changed the nature of this work leading to serious questions about the future of this industry. A mixed‐methods survey was conducted with Africa‐based CMS ( n = 107) who responded to several open‐ended questions related to their perceptions of AI and its potential use in content moderation. Thematic analysis revealed strong support for the use of AI in content moderation. However, CMs noted several barriers to AI implementation, such as an inability to apply context, which limits its efficacy. The findings suggest that African CMs appreciate the potential benefits that AI can offer to the content moderation industry, yet still see a clear need for AI to be balanced with human oversight to properly address the contextual nuance that is inherent to the role.

articles.title: Masking or lexicographic preferences? Using conjoint experiments to distinguish between two fundamental theories of choice
articles.abstract: Many studies on candidate choice and other political preferences suggest that the effect of one attribute may mask the effect of another attribute, which the respondent has no information about. If, for instance, respondents lack information about party membership, they may infer that female candidates are Democrats, which would lead to biased estimates of the pure effect of candidate gender. We propose an alternative explanation—namely that respondents have lexicographic preferences—and we present an empirical test using conjoint experiments to distinguish between what we call pure masking and lexicographic preferences. We illustrate our method using data on the effect of gender, race, and party in candidate choice and replicate the results in a preregistered conjoint experiment. We offer recommendations for researchers studying candidate and political choices.

articles.title: ROUGE: A database of disaster impacts in the Global South using Red Cross reports and Large Language Models
articles.authors: Laura Hasbini, Luca Gaetan Severino, Mariana Madruga de Brito, Gabriela Chiquito Gesualdo, Ana Maria Rotaru, David Niklaus Bresch, Evelyn Mühlhofer, Jingxian Wang, Taís Maria Nunes Carvalho
articles.abstract: High quality data on natural hazard damages are crucial for effective disaster risk management. Yet, existing impact datasets remain limited and often biased toward Northern countries and monetary losses. To help address these gaps, we present ROUGE (Redcross Operations Unified Global Emergency database); a new socio-economic impact database obtained using textual operational reports from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. These reports are systematically collected and provide broad coverage of regions that are commonly underrepresented in existing impact datasets. Using large language models, we extract qualitative and quantitative information on a wide range of non-monetary impacts at national and sub-national scales. The resulting dataset documents socio-economic impacts of natural hazards on the population, infrastructure and economy with a spatial detail reaching the subregional level. This resource is designed to support research and applications that require geographically explicit information on socio-economic impacts of disasters, enabling more precise and inclusive analyses of socio-economic consequences of natural hazards worldwide.

articles.title: A global dataset of immigration flow composition by age, sex and educational attainment
articles.abstract: People at different ages and with different educational background have different migration patterns. However, international migration flows by age and educational attainment are scarce and not always comparable. We use a super learning algorithm with multiple initial models to estimate age and education composition of male and female immigrants for 199 countries over six five-year periods from 1990–1995 to 2015–2020. We access the performance of our approach through cross-validation and comparing initial learners with the super learner algorithm using multiple evaluation metrics. We also compare our age composition estimates against equivalent measures from Eurostat. The estimates indicate that while the proportion of immigration flows with higher education increase in all regions, Europe has the highest immigration flow with secondary or higher education.

articles.title: National security versus human security: Intrastate conflict and states’ rhetoric on conventional arms control in the United Nations general assembly
articles.abstract: While arms control during the Cold War was primarily concerned with weapons of mass destruction and their role in national security, the end of the bipolar order shifted attention toward intrastate conflicts, the conventional weapons with which they are fought, and their humanitarian consequences for civilian populations. Yet we still lack systematic evidence on how governments directly involved in such conflicts perceive conventional arms control. I argue that acute intrastate conflicts, but not intractable conflicts, lead states to view conventional arms control primarily as a matter of national security rather than a humanitarian issue. I test this argument quantitatively, using data on states’ rhetorical positions on conventional arms control in the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) and on enduring internal rivalries (EIRs). Consistent with my expectations, I find that intrastate conflicts unrelated to EIRs are associated with a stronger emphasis on national security in UNGA speeches, whereas conflicts embedded in EIRs are not significantly related to states’ rhetoric on conventional arms control. These findings shed new light on the relationship between intrastate conflict and arms control.

articles.title: Reassurance and betrayal: Cross-ethnic appeals by party leaders in divided societies lead to asymmetric voter reactions
articles.abstract: Why do conciliatory political appeals sometimes polarise rather than moderate electoral competition in divided societies? Existing accounts of consociational power-sharing explain how hardline parties can become credible negotiators, but they say less about how voters respond when the leaders of displaced moderate parties attempt to broaden support beyond their traditional community. I argue that leaders’ cross-ethnic appeals function as reassurance signalling: they reduce perceived threat to the outgroup while simultaneously weakening perceptions of defensive credibility among co-ethnics. Voters therefore update leader evaluations in opposite directions relative to a party’s inherited reputation. Using survey data from the 2022 Northern Ireland Assembly election, I compare leader evaluations to party baselines across identity groups. A leader who emphasised cross-community accommodation was evaluated more favourably by the opposing community and less favourably by co-ethnics, while leaders emphasising intra-group defence did not exhibit this pattern. The findings suggest moderation in divided societies redistributes support across groups rather than uniformly increasing approval, providing a behavioural mechanism within post-tribune party competition.

articles.title: Constructing Online Harms: How “Trust and Safety” Translates Safety Into Risk
articles.abstract: How are online harms recognized and prioritized within platform companies? Academics, journalists, and regulators have focused on identifying how digital platforms produce dangerous effects, but how harms are constructed within these organizations remains largely opaque. Based on 42 interviews with Trust and Safety specialists—the workers who define, operationalize, and create mechanisms to prevent or mitigate harmful effects—and ethnographic observation of industry forums, I describe how these workers transform concerns about platform dangers into actionable rules and processes. First, they position themselves as advocates for users, claiming moral authority to represent them within their organizations. Second, they translate abstract concerns into concrete organizational risks. Third, they publicize their companies’ harm-mitigation efforts in industry forums, performing responsiveness to critics and distributing responsibility across the sector. User harms become organizationally visible when they can be translated into corporate risks—legal liability, reputational damage, or revenue threats—and technical problems.

articles.title: Political Fracturing within the Asian American Electorate
articles.abstract: Racial minority political influence may be jeopardized when constituent subgroups disagree on policy priorities and on the political parties that best represent their interests. In this study, we examine the prevalence of political fracturing— the formation of pluralistic subgroups that coalesce around political ideology, identity, trust, engagement, and issue opinions within broader racial groups—within the Asian American electorate, an increasingly influential minority group. We capitalize on granular data from the 2016 Collaborative Multiracial Post-Election Survey to assess the prevalence and characterizing features of political fracturing, and we test several possible explanations of political fracturing among Asian Americans, especially those that relate to ethnic variation within the Asian American electorate. Latent class analysis uncovers three distinct classes of roughly equal sizes that broadly align with liberal, conservative, and politically ambivalent groups. Logistic regressions reveal that class membership is predicted by respondent ethnicity, and that age, education, income, and religious identification partly explain effects from ethnicity. These findings uncover evidence of political fracturing among Asian Americans that is not captured by isolated analyses of issue opinion and political participation and suggest that a focus on broad racial categories in minority group politics research may mask considerable political subgroup heterogeneity within minority racial groups.

articles.title: Home Country Influence or Local Issues?—A Study of New York State Senate District 17 Elections in 2022 and 2024
articles.abstract: Do American voters of East Asian immigrant backgrounds decide their vote choice based on international issues related to their home countries, or are immigrant-dense communities focused on domestic issues like most American voters? We evaluate these questions using two state senate elections (2022 and 2024) in a highly dense immigrant district (17th State Senate District, Brooklyn, New York), comparing the electoral impact of a high-salience international issue (Taiwan) against a divisive domestic issue (a proposed homeless shelter). We develop measures for both factors and test them with precinct-level data. We find that despite the high share of immigrant-background voters and growing attention to the Taiwan issue in American politics in recent years, the homeless shelter issue dominated the subnational electoral politics of this district. We buttress these results with two analyses of East Asian CMPS respondents, finding that domestic economic issues are more important to these voters than international concerns.

articles.title: Biracial at the Ballot Box: Exploring the Association Between Interracial Relationships and Political Beliefs
articles.authors: Byron Miller, Madelyn Chandler, Nico Allen
articles.abstract: Despite the tremendous influence politicians have over the lives of the growing number of people in interracial relationships in the United States, little is known about the political beliefs of interracially partnered individuals. Using nationally representative data from the Add Health Study, we find people in interracial relationships generally have more liberal political views than those in same-race relationships, but differences are moderated by the individual’s race/ethnicity, sex, and marital status. Specifically, interracially partnered women have liberal-leaning beliefs, but individuals who are Asian, Hispanic, and married have more conservative-leaning views. Three-way interactions further reveal interracially married Asian and Black persons both have more liberal-leaning political beliefs. The impact the growing prevalence of interracial relationships may have on the future evolution of American political representation and policies is discussed.

articles.title: Can a public information campaign increase trust in American elections?
articles.authors: Thad Kousser, Seth J. Hill, Neil Malhotra, Robert M. Stein
articles.abstract: Confidence in the conduct and results of American elections has declined and polarized along party lines in recent years. Can a nonpartisan public information campaign featuring election officials enhance trust in elections when delivered to skeptical voters during a contentious political contest? We analyze a preregistered, randomized field experiment conducted during the 2024 US presidential election in which conservative voters were randomly assigned to a control condition or to receive a multimodal messaging campaign designed by political professionals explaining protections on election integrity. In contrast to the large positive effects of informational messages found in recent survey experiments, we observed primarily null effects with respect to turnout ( n = 147,488), general confidence in elections ( n = 4740 to 4868), and perceptions of the frequency of fraud ( n = 4925). We observed one hypothesized effect: an increase in trust in the vote-by-mail process ( n = 6438). This study provides rigorous evidence from a real public information campaign on election integrity, yielding effect sizes in the field that are much smaller than those observed in prior survey settings.

articles.title: The Media Bias Detector: A framework for annotating and analyzing the news
articles.authors: Samar Haider, Amir Tohidi, Jenny S. Wang, Timothy Dörr, David M. Rothschild, Chris Callison-Burch, Duncan J. Watts
articles.abstract: News organizations introduce bias into their coverage via the choices they make about which topics to cover (or ignore) and how to frame the issues they do decide to cover. Here, we introduce the Media Bias Detector, a scalable computational framework that integrates large language models (LLMs) with near-real-time news scraping to extract structured annotations, including political lean, tone, topics, article type, and major events, across hundreds of articles per day. We quantify these dimensions of coverage at the sentence level, the article level, and the publisher level, expanding the ways in which researchers can analyze selection and framing bias in the modern news landscape. We also release an interactive web platform for convenient exploration of these data and an accompanying dataset covering more than 140,000 articles published in 2024 by 10 prominent publishers. Last, we present some results derived from this dataset that illustrate how the MBD can uncover correlates of bias in news coverage.
